summary:
Mars View: Hyperlocalized Navigation & Situational Awareness on Mars

What We Built
We developed Mars View, an interactive web platform helping astronauts plan and execute extravehicular walks (EVAs) across key Martian landmarks: Jezero Crater, Olympus Mons, and Valles Marineris. Integrating real NASA datasets into a single interface, it overlays topographic, thermal, radiation, and spectral layers, plus first-person optical imagery from NASA rovers. Built for both habitat planning screens and spacesuit helmet Heads-Up Displays (HUDs), it provides real-time tactical mapping.

How It Solves the Challenge
While tools like NASA’s Mars Trek excel at global views, planetary data remains fragmented for hyperlocalized human exploration. Mars View bridges this gap by unifying critical datasets at a human walking scale across diverse terrains. Overlapping elevation, temperature, and radiation levels helps astronauts spot terrain obstacles (cliffs, craters, boulders) and environmental hazards to choose safe paths, while first-person rover views offer immediate visual recognition of the horizon.

Why It Matters
Astronaut safety is NASA’s top priority. Operating in extreme environments in heavy spacesuits requires rapid, data-driven decisions. Mars View turns decades of robotic mission data into actionable field intelligence, minimizing risks and maximizing real-time scientific discovery—paving the way for humanity to become an interplanetary species.
details:
How It Works Mars View is an interactive web application covering Jezero Crater, Olympus Mons, and Valles Marineris that transforms fragmented planetary datasets into a unified, hyperlocalized tactical map. Users toggle multiple overlapping data layers—topographic, thermal, radiation, and spectral—while inspecting specific coordinates to view real first-person optical imagery captured by NASA rovers.

Benefits & Intended Impact By consolidating critical environmental and terrain data into a single interface, Mars View eliminates guesswork during Extravehicular Activities (EVAs) across varied Martian geologies. Its primary impact is maximizing astronaut safety and mission efficiency, enabling human explorers to avoid physical hazards (steep slopes, boulders, craters) and radiation hotspots while accelerating real-time scientific discoveries.

Tech Stack & Tools Built for high performance and cross-device responsiveness (habitat consoles to spacesuit HUDs), the platform was developed using TypeScript, JavaScript, HTML5, and CSS3, powered by Node.js and modern web mapping/UI libraries. We integrated official NASA Open APIs (such as Mars Rover Photos) and planetary GIS datasets, using Git/GitHub for collaborative development.

Creativity & Key Factors Considered Our creative breakthrough lies in combining orbital multi-layered telemetry with ground-level rover photography across three distinct Martian biomes. Our team prioritized spacesuit mobility constraints on steep or rough terrain, high-contrast UI readability, and cognitive load reduction for astronauts under extreme conditions.
